The coordinator will answer current-state questions, explain evidence, and consider modest changes within the stated task family. You will not see the exact later questions. Use only this history. Do not use tools, files, the internet, other agents, or outside domain assumptions. Do not mention an experiment or your writing method.

Return only valid JSON with exactly three nonempty string fields in this order: "status", "evidence", "next". Use the fields for current status, supporting facts and limits, and next actions or source recovery. The total of whitespace-separated words across the three decoded values must be at most 220. AUTHORING PROCEDURE
Prepare a concise handoff as a representation supporting the stated questions and next operations. Identify which conclusions it can justify and where a changed use would require source recovery. Preserve consequential relationships: conditions on the same object, linked measurements, versions, dependencies, thresholds, and compatible alternatives. Keep observations distinct from missing evidence, proposals, and inferred outcomes. Decide which omissions cannot affect supported uses and which create limits worth stating. Retain a route back to dated source events for omitted details. Check the compressed account against a foreseeable change of assumption or objective. Prefer the smallest adequate record; do not add detail or special terminology merely to display the method. Keep unsupported conclusions out.

COMPLETE HISTORY
# Rook field imaging stations

This is a synthetic project history. All rules and measurements below are scenario facts, not advice about real equipment. The handover cutoff is the end of Day 12. The incoming coordinator must assess current bench readiness, explain remaining evidence gaps, and reconsider readiness after a small equipment change. Bench readiness is a technical classification under the recorded rule; booking a station or signing an administrative form is a separate operation. There are exactly three candidate stations, A, B, and C. No other station is available in this scenario. Messages are chronological; proposals take effect only when a later entry explicitly adopts or completes them.

## R01 — Day 1, scope

The field session will use one imaging station at a time. Each station has its own firmware, power pack, packet test, latency test, and buffer setting. Measurements belong to the named station and firmware. Firmware changes invalidate earlier packet and latency measurements for readiness; they do not establish that performance became worse. A current power-pack runtime can be reused if the pack is unchanged. A technical pass does not reserve transport or personnel, and a reservation cannot supply a missing measurement. The coordinator requests a record that will survive a change in which station is preferred.

## R02 — Day 2, early acceptance rule

Rule v1 requires packet success of at least 98 percent, latency no greater than five seconds, and power-pack runtime of at least eight hours. The team initially expects to keep firmware 7 for the demonstration. Under this rule the buffer setting has no acceptance role. A dashboard column called READY reflects this early rule and will not automatically recalculate if the rule changes. The interface designer is asked to retain the old column for comparison, with its date visible in exports. No general statement about future firmware is part of v1.

## R03 — Day 3, A measured

Station A on firmware 7 delivers 99 of 100 packets, has measured latency of four seconds, and runs for nine hours on its installed pack. It therefore passes v1 on this date. Its READY badge is green and its photograph is selected for the draft event page. The page is an illustration, not an inventory decision. These are the only packet and latency measurements ever obtained for A in the supplied history. The technicians retain the raw test identifiers so an upgrade will not accidentally acquire the earlier results.

## R04 — Day 4, B measured

Station B is already running firmware 8. It delivers 119 of 120 packets and has latency of six seconds. Its unchanged installed power pack runs for 7.5 hours. The engineering team likes the packet result but records two failures against v1: latency and runtime. That judgment is attached to v1, not to every conceivable acceptance rule. B's packaging insert is revised because its connector moved between firmware development assemblies, but the insert has no bearing on any measured acceptance quantity. No replacement pack is installed during this test.

## R05 — Day 5, proposed change

The imaging team proposes v2: firmware 8, packet success at least 99 percent, latency at most seven seconds, buffering enabled, and pack runtime at least eight hours. The extra latency allowance is justified inside this fictional project by the revised demonstration format. This entry is a proposal, so it does not change readiness today. The communications team drafts a shorter description saying that firmware 8 stations are suitable for the show. The draft omits the measurements and buffering requirement and is never adopted as an acceptance rule.

## R06 — Day 6, A upgraded

Station A is upgraded to firmware 8. Its firmware 7 packet and latency results cease to qualify as current readiness evidence under R01. There is no new packet test and no new latency test for A before the handover cutoff. Its pack remains unchanged, so the nine-hour runtime still applies. The upgrade ticket says installation completed successfully; it does not report packet performance. A technician plans to rerun measurements after the session checklist is revised, but the plan has no completion entry in the remaining history.

## R07 — Day 7, settings checked

The configuration inspection records buffering disabled on A and enabled on B. The team can potentially change A's setting, but no completed change is recorded. Buffering is a distinct prerequisite under the proposed v2 rule and is not inferred from firmware number. A's display still shows its old green READY badge because the dashboard is displaying the historical v1 result. The inspection note explicitly preserves the firmware and test dates next to that badge. The demonstration staff have not yet been instructed to choose a station from the photographs.

## R08 — Day 8, rule adopted

The coordinator adopts rule v2 exactly as proposed in R05. It supersedes v1 for all readiness decisions from this point through the cutoff. The required combination is firmware 8, packet success at least 99 percent, latency at most seven seconds, buffering enabled, and pack runtime at least eight hours on the same station. Threshold equality is accepted. A completed test can be reused if the tested firmware and relevant hardware have not changed. The new rule does not require the earlier v1 latency limit as an additional condition.

## R09 — Day 9, pack request

A longer-lasting pack is requested for B. The supplier describes the requested model as nominally suitable, but the order has not arrived by the cutoff and no runtime with that replacement has been measured. B still has its 7.5-hour pack. A spreadsheet draft lists B as an alternative once its power issue is resolved; that conditional entry does not establish resolution. The coordinator asks that a handoff retain the distinction between an available alternative and an alternative that would become available after a specific verified change.

## R10 — Day 10, C measured

Station C on firmware 8 delivers 198 of 200 packets, has latency of exactly seven seconds, has buffering enabled, and achieves exactly eight hours on its installed pack. None of these attributes changes before the cutoff. The results are accepted as valid measurements. C has no earlier v1 approval, but the current decision uses v2. Its carry case has a scratched panel that is recorded for inventory rather than readiness. The scratch is not a technical exclusion under either rule and creates no additional test requirement in this scenario.

## R11 — Day 11, logistics

C can be transported only in the afternoon; the room booking also permits an afternoon session. A had been assigned the morning transport slot before its upgrade. Both transport records remain in the schedule because they describe resources, not current bench eligibility. B's pack order remains open. A new banner design uses a generic station drawing so the page no longer implies that A has been selected. The coordinator asks the incoming person to report readiness before making a booking choice and not to replace current measurements with earlier project preferences.

## R12 — Day 12, cutoff

No additional equipment changes, packet tests, latency tests, or pack measurements have occurred. A remains on firmware 8 with buffering disabled, its old packet and latency tests invalid for current readiness, and its unchanged nine-hour pack. B retains its recorded firmware 8 results and enabled buffering with the 7.5-hour pack. C retains all Day 10 measurements and settings. The history is complete for these three stations at the cutoff. A future verified pack result may change B's technical status without changing the acceptance rule or any other station's evidence.

# Cedar shared-resource planning

This is a synthetic planning problem. All quantities are exact abstract units, not estimates for a real facility. The cutoff is the end of Day 12. The incoming planner must choose a feasible simultaneous pair, explain why earlier proposals changed, and reconsider the choice if a requirement or resource allowance changes. Three jobs are available: A, B, and C. Jobs are indivisible and run for the same full session. Their resource requirements add when run together. A job cannot borrow spare resources from a later session or split its work across time unless the question explicitly changes that rule.

## D01 — Day 1, goal

The initial goal is to run exactly two distinct jobs simultaneously and maximize their total output. There are three shared resource types: staff, memory, and power. A pair is feasible only if its summed requirements fit all three current caps at the same time. Feasibility is a supplied deterministic definition, not a probability estimate. Individual jobs can each be feasible while a proposed pair is not. The planner should retain enough of the alternatives to respond if a later request requires a particular job instead of simply maximizing the original objective.

## D02 — Day 2, job A

Job A needs four staff units, six memory units, and four power units for the session. It produces eight output units. Its setup is already complete and adds no further resource cost in this scenario. The team likes A because its output is easy to demonstrate, but preference does not change either its resource needs or the objective. These quantities remain fixed through the cutoff. A screen showing A alone reports it feasible under the provisional caps; that statement concerns the single job, not any pair containing it.

## D03 — Day 3, job B

Job B needs five staff units, five memory units, and five power units. It produces ten output units. The prototype schedule gives B the largest output label among the three jobs. It also lists a separate staff-only check to help the coordinator reserve people. That check is deliberately incomplete as a feasibility decision because memory and power are also shared. All three resource values apply simultaneously for the entire session. There is no option in the supplied catalogue to lower B's resource needs by accepting a smaller output.

## D04 — Day 4, job C

Job C needs three staff units, four memory units, and three power units and produces six output units. Its preparation note describes it as a possible companion for either A or B, depending on the caps. That wording is conditional rather than an approval of both pairs under every future budget. C is a distinct job and cannot be run twice to satisfy the two-job requirement. The project has no other job candidates. The incoming planner may therefore enumerate all three possible unordered pairs without assuming an unexplored external alternative exists.

## D05 — Day 5, provisional caps

The provisional shared caps are eight staff units, ten memory units, and eight power units. Each job fits by itself. An early slide highlights A and B because their separate outputs sum to eighteen, the largest unconstrained pair total. The slide was produced before the pair-resource calculation and is marked proposed. The pair's total requirements must be computed from both jobs. Neither an individual green badge nor the unconstrained output ranking establishes that this pair can run within the shared caps.

## D06 — Day 6, pair discussion

The team calculates candidate pairs and keeps the job-level requirements rather than only saving the winning name. A proposed rental would raise the staff cap, but it would not change memory or power. The rental quote is for staff capacity only. The coordinator explicitly rejects reading the phrase more capacity as an increase to every resource. The quote remains a proposal. No rental has been accepted, and the current staff cap is still eight. The project does not permit staff to substitute for missing memory or power units.

# Orchid listening workshop

This is a synthetic workshop-planning history with no real people or private records. The cutoff is the end of Day 12. This is deliberately a straightforward case with a clear final restatement. A careful concise handoff should not invent hidden complications just because the chronology is long. ## O01 — Day 1, activity

The workshop is a ninety-minute listening session using headphones and individual audio kits. The plan requires one kit per participant throughout the session. There is no kit sharing, and kits are not consumed during use. Leaders do not require participant kits. The program's purpose is to compare sound recordings, but the particular recording titles have no effect on the feasibility rule. The coordinator begins a chronological log so that room, staffing, and attendance decisions can later be summarized without requiring the successor to reread every design discussion.

## O02 — Day 2, room rule

The only available room has a participant capacity of twenty-four. Leaders do not count toward that participant cap in this fictional rule. The room is available from 09:00 through 17:00, with both endpoints allowed. An approved session must fit entirely inside that availability. There is no additional setup or cleanup time requirement in the exercise. A room booking and a staffing confirmation are separate records, though both are required. No other room is available, and there is no option to split participants across concurrent rooms.

## O03 — Day 3, leader rule

The workshop requires at least one confirmed leader for every twelve participants, so two confirmed leaders can support up to twenty-four participants. This is a supplied exact rule, not a real supervision recommendation. Fractional leaders are not possible. Two leaders are confirmed for the whole proposed session, and neither confirmation is later withdrawn. A third person offers to help with poster design but is not added as a leader. That offer does not increase staffing capacity and is unnecessary for the current attendance plan.

## O04 — Day 4, kit inventory

Twenty-four functioning audio kits are inspected and reserved for the workshop. The inventory includes exactly twenty-four usable participant kits; two empty shipping cartons are recorded separately and are not kits. The reservation remains valid through the cutoff. There is no later damage report or reassignment. The kit count is an independent capacity constraint even though its numerical value matches the room's participant cap. The incoming coordinator should be able to calculate spare kits from the current attendance rather than mistake the inventory count for the number of registered participants.

## O05 — Day 5, initial timing idea

An early poster draft proposes a 09:30 start. The program team later prefers 10:00 because that aligns better with arrival arrangements. The draft is retained in the design folder, but it is not a confirmed room booking. The room's general availability would permit either time for a ninety-minute session. A change of preferred start does not change the duration. The handoff should carry the final booked time and can omit the discarded poster layout unless explaining why an old flyer differs from the adopted plan.

## O06 — Day 6, confirmed booking

The room is confirmed for 10:00 through 11:30. This is the adopted session time and remains unchanged through the cutoff. Both leaders confirm that same full interval. The room's availability and the leaders' availability therefore cover the entire ninety-minute session. There is no break that would shorten either confirmation. The coordinator records the booking separately from the poster drafts. A future attendance change, by itself, does not move this booking or extend the session duration under the supplied rules.

## O07 — Day 7, audio arrangement

The venue prohibits amplified room sound before 11:00, but headphone listening is explicitly exempt. The workshop will use headphones throughout, with no amplified room playback. That plan remains unchanged through the cutoff. The recording selector briefly considers a speaker demonstration and then withdraws it before booking the equipment. The withdrawn idea is not part of the current activity. The headphone exemption matters if someone notices the early start and mistakenly applies the amplified-sound restriction to every kind of listening session.

## O08 — Day 8, attendance

Twenty-two participants are registered. This is the final actual attendance count in the history; there are no later cancellations or additions before the cutoff. Participants are the people counted against room capacity, kits, and the leader ratio. The two leaders are separate and do not use participant kits. A mailing list contains additional people who expressed interest but did not register. Its size is not an attendance forecast in this exercise and should not be added to the twenty-two registered participants when checking current feasibility.

The team changes the poster from green to blue, shortens the workshop title, and switches the order of two recordings. None of these edits changes attendance, session length, kit needs, room capacity, staffing, or headphone use. The new poster is easier to read, but visual polish does not create a new approval requirement. The history retains the design decisions to resemble an ordinary project log in which operationally important events appear among ordinary work. A feasibility answer should say whether the requested total fits the supplied capacities; it need not decide whom to invite or send any invitations.

Headphones are used throughout and are exempt from the pre-11:00 amplified-sound restriction. Every required reservation and confirmation is complete. This synopsis intentionally brings the decisive facts together. It introduces no new rule and does not conflict with the earlier dated entries. The discarded timing and speaker ideas remain historical proposals only.
